offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 5000/-, in default rigorous imprisonment for one year
physical_harm: The deceased had incised wounds on her body, indicating severe injuries caused by a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword
key_evidence_accepted: There was oral, medical and documentary evidence which undoubtedly connected the accused with the murder. The post-mortem report made it abundantly clear that all the injuries found on the deceased were incised wounds, which could be caused with a sharp edged weapon such as a sword. The appellant failed to give any explanation for his presence in the room of the deceased and the presence of blood stained sword in his hand.
witness_credibility: The courts below concluded that the name of the husband of the deceased may have been the result of confusion in the mind of PW10. The conclusion reached by both the courts below on due appreciation of the evidence of these two witnesses cannot be said to be either unjustified or perverse. The version given by PW 11 is consistent with the testimony of the Investigating Officer PW.13.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant opened the door when the police arrived and stated that he killed the deceased. He was holding blood stained sword in his hand and his clothes were blood stained.

legal_representation.accused: K.T.S. Tusli, Ram Nivas, Raj Kamal, A.P. Dhamija, Sanjeev Malhotra
legal_representation.state: C.D. Singh, Sunny Choudhary, Shashank Parihar, Sakshi Kakkar

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was the step mother of the appellant and that the appellant was present at the scene of the crime. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's presence in the room where the deceased was found dead with incised wounds, the blood-stained sword in his hand, and his clothes being blood-stained. The prosecution also highlighted the post-mortem report indicating the nature of the injuries, which could have been caused by a sharp-edged weapon like a sword.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant was falsely implicated and that the real culprit was being shielded. The appellant claimed he was already in police custody at the time of the murder and had been beaten up by the police, necessitating medical examination. The defence also questioned the reliability of the FIR and the credibility of the evidence, suggesting that the prosecution's case was weak and based on incomplete or unreliable information.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in cases where the prosecution relies primarily on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully established, consistent with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt, and exclude every other hypothesis. The courts must ensure that the evidence forms a complete chain that leaves no reasonable ground for the accused's innocence.
precedent_relied_upon: Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P. 1952 SCR 1091; Rangaiah v. State of Karnataka (2008) 16 SCC 737; Ghurey /al v. State of UP (2008) 10 SCC 450; Abdulwahab Abdulmajid Baloch v. State of Gujrat (2009) 11 SCC 625; Budh Singh v. State of UP (2006) 9 SCC 731; Rajeevan v. State of Kera/a (2003) 3 SCC 355; Oharamver & ors. v. State of U.P (2010) 4 SCC 469; Rabindra Mahto v. State of Jharkhand (2006) 10 SCC 432; Aqeel Ahmed v. State of UP (2008) 16 SCC 372
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the courts below, including the High Court, found the appellant guilty of murder based on the circumstantial evidence, which was deemed sufficient to establish his guilt. The Supreme Court confirmed the conviction and sentence as being in line with the established legal principles.
